newsitem.title: USA: Flood threat builds in upper Midwest United States.
newsitem.headline: Flood threat builds in upper Midwest United States.

text.p: Authorities increased flood preparations in the upper Midwest Monday in anticipation of warmer weather causing record-high snow packs to melt.
Thousands of sandbags were being filled in South Dakota where Gov. Bill Janklow warned residents record flooding was imminent.
"Right now it's a waiting game," a spokesman for the governor said, adding that forecasts of milder temperatures made it likely the flood threat would increase this week.

The Sioux Falls area, the most heavily populated region threatened by the impending melt, was working to build up dikes protecting the city from the Big Sioux River. Flooding was also likely along the Vermillion and James rivers.
Lyle Johnson, director of public works for Sioux Falls, told Reuters that dikes were being raised by as much as 3 feet in some places.
"Our record flood here was in 1969," he said, "but the moisture content of the snow upstream from here is higher than it was in 1969, so we're taking these precautions."

The dikes and spillways system protecting the city held during the 1969 high water. South Dakota officials asked gasoline stations, grain elevators, factories and other commercial operations in flood-prone areas to make sure no chemicals were released in the event of high water.

A succession of blizzards hit parts of eastern South Dakota and western Minnesota during the winter and generally cold weather has kept most of the snow on the ground. But Thursday is the first day of spring and warmer conditions were forecast across the region in the next few days.

Minnesota and Wisconsin this weekend reported four more snowmobile-related deaths, bringing to 64 the number of such fatalities in the two states this winter. Officials said alcohol played a role in many of the deaths during the season.

Parts of central Wisconsin got more than two feet of snow late last week. The same storm left a wide section of lower Michigan covered in ice, downing power lines and blacking out as many as a quarter million homes and businesses. Consumers Energy, a unit of CMS Energy Corp, reported that about 25,000 customers were still without power because of the ice.
To the south, the Ohio River was falling after a two-week rampage along parts of five states. The flood crest passed the junction of the Ohio and Mississippi rivers during the weekend.
More rain was forecast for the Ohio Valley this week but not in amounts likely to cause additional flooding.
